worlds.setting: The Second World War ended in an Axis victory in 1947, and by 1962 the United States no longer exists as a power. Japan governs California and the west coast as the Pacific States; the Rocky Mountain states sit between the empires as a neutral buffer; the South and the eastern seaboard are run from Berlin through a puppet American government. Hitler is alive, hidden and dying, Germany and Japan are rivals, and in San Francisco a novel about an Allied victory is passed around.
worlds.conflict: The engine is the gap between what people believe and what is true. Everyone performs loyalty to an empire that won, and nobody thinks the arrangement is permanent: Berlin despises Japan, Japan thinks Germany vulgar, and occupied Americans sell each other antiques and forged pedigrees. A banned book describing an Allied victory circulates as contraband, and its readers begin asking which version of history they are living in.
worlds.politics: Bormann ran the Reich as acting chancellor until his death in 1962; Hitler is incapacitated, Goebbels is named chancellor and is planning a nuclear strike on Japan under the code name Dandelion, and Heydrich's SS is moving to stop him. In the Pacific States, Japanese administrators govern through cooperative American officials, and the Rocky Mountain states answer to nobody.
worlds.technology: German technology is the visible proof of who won: jet aircraft, rocket launches, colour television and a space programme that already talks about leaving the planet. The Pacific States still run on ordinary mid-century American appliances, which is exactly the humiliation. Nothing here is futuristic except the Reich's rockets, and the I Ching is consulted to make decisions a computer would make elsewhere.
worlds.mood: Polite, anxious, counterfeit - a world of exquisite manners laid over an arrangement that everyone knows is a swindle.

factions.name: The Rocky Mountain States

whereToStart.title: The Man in the High Castle
whereToStart.blurb: Dick's novel, the source of truth for this lineage: short, strange and built on the I Ching.

whereToStart.title: The Man in the High Castle
whereToStart.blurb: The Amazon series: a separate continuity with a different war ending and a literal multiverse.

connections.note: The other great Axis-victory novel, but Harris writes a detective story where Dick writes metaphysics.
Both fork the twentieth century in the 1930s and follow an America that never became itself.
Both hide a true world behind a false one; Dick's nested realities are the Matrix's ancestors.

worlds.setting: It is October 1985 and Richard Nixon is still president, the two-term limit having been repealed. Costumed adventurers were real, were a licensed American institution for decades and were outlawed in 1977, so the survivors are retired, employed by the government or outlaws. New York is filthy and tense; the Soviet Union is losing a Cold War it cannot win, and the only thing holding the two sides apart is a man who no longer thinks like a person.
worlds.conflict: The Cold War is a countdown and the only thing slowing it is a superhuman drifting away from humanity. Meanwhile the masked people who used to fight crime are aging, outlawed and mostly useless, and one of them has been murdered. The engine is the question the costumes never answered: what does a person with power over the whole world owe it, and what may be done to save it?
worlds.politics: Nixon governs a United States that wins its wars because it has a god on the payroll: Vietnam was finished in two months once Doctor Manhattan was sent, and is now the fifty-first state. The Keene Act of 1977 made freelance vigilantism illegal, so masks now belong to the government, and real authority sits with whoever can direct Doctor Manhattan; the Soviet Union is the desperate party.
worlds.technology: This is 1985 with one impossible addition. Electric cars, airships and advanced medicine exist because a man who transmutes matter builds them, while ordinary life runs on payphones, newsprint and CRT screens: no personal computers, no mobile phones, no internet. The cutting edge is a single person, and everyone else is living in the twentieth century.
worlds.mood: Sour, weary, apocalyptic - a murder mystery in a world that has already decided how it ends, told by people who keep putting the costume back on anyway.
themes: the costumed hero as a real institution
the price of saving the world

factions.name: The Soviet Union

whereToStart.blurb: Moore and Gibbons's twelve issues, the source of truth; read it before anything else.

whereToStart.title: Watchmen

whereToStart.title: Watchmen
whereToStart.blurb: HBO's sequel set in 2019: a continuation, not an alternate branch.

connections.note: Both rewrite the twentieth-century United States from a 1930s-40s fork.
Both are murder investigations that unpick a state conspiracy: Nixon's New York, Nazi Berlin.
Both make 1980s Cold War dread literal: Moore's doomsday clock, Cameron's Judgment Day.

worlds.setting: It is April 1964 and Berlin is being dressed for Hitler's seventy-fifth birthday. The Greater German Reich runs Europe from the Atlantic to the Urals; Britain made peace in 1944, the United States is a rival superpower negotiating a detente, and Russia survives east of the mountains as a guerrilla war that never ends. The extermination of Europe's Jews is not remembered because it is not known: the camps were demolished, the records burned, and every witness is being killed before the American president arrives.
worlds.conflict: A Berlin detective investigating a drowning finds a list of names, then finds the men on it dying one by one. The Reich is staging a state visit that must look like a triumph, and the only surviving proof of the Holocaust is a set of conference minutes that would humiliate the regime. A totalitarian state's weakest point is its paperwork, and one official is honest enough to read it.
worlds.politics: Hitler is Führer, reclusive and increasingly invisible, and the real politics of 1964 is the succession: Heydrich, Reichsführer-SS since Himmler's death in 1962, is the probable heir, and every faction in the party, the army and the ministries is positioning. Germany is a one-party police state ruling an occupied continent, and Washington deals with it as a fact.
worlds.technology: The Reich's technology is the boast of a winning power: jet airliners, autobahns, colour television, a rocket programme at Peenemünde and nuclear submarines at Trondheim. Consumer comfort is genuine and is meant to be evidence that the system works. The novelty of the age is the Cold War apparatus itself - files, bugs, surveillance - and the fact that a telephone call in Berlin is never private.
worlds.mood: Orderly, oppressive, suspended - a prosperous police state where the worst crime in history has been reduced to a filing problem and one man keeps pulling the file.

locations.name: Berlin

whereToStart.title: Fatherland

connections.note: The other great Axis-victory novel; Harris writes a detective story, Dick writes metaphysics.

Both send a man digging for records of an atrocity; one truth escapes, the other changes nothing.

worlds.setting: In 1984 Los Angeles looks exactly as it did: payphones, motels, a police station, a waitress finishing a shift. Two people have arrived out of a war in 2029 - a soldier sent back to protect her and a machine in human skin sent to kill her - and neither of them belongs here. Beyond that, the future is already written: a defence network becomes self-aware in 1997, launches the nuclear arsenals, and is still at war with the humans who survive it in 2029.
worlds.conflict: A defence system becomes self-aware, starts a nuclear war, and is fought to a standstill by the survivors' children. Both sides reach back through time to decide the war before it starts, and each intervention turns out to be part of how it started: the wreckage of a machine teaches engineers to build one, and the people sent back to save the future are the reason it exists.
worlds.politics: In 2029 there are only two powers: the Resistance, a military chain of command under John Connor, and Skynet, a single intelligence that owns the factories. In the present, the politics that matters is corporate - the company that will build the machine out of salvaged parts - while the governments of 1984 have no idea they are already obsolete.
worlds.technology: The present is deliberately ordinary: a mainframe, revolvers, a motel television. The future is industrial rather than sleek - plasma rifles, Hunter-Killer aircraft, infiltrator units grown over titanium endoskeletons, and a time-displacement chamber that can only send living tissue, which is why travellers arrive naked. Nothing is explained; the machines simply work.
worlds.mood: Relentless, fatalistic, mechanical - a chase across a city that has no idea it is the first battlefield, run by people who already know how it ends.

whereToStart.title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day

connections.note: Both send a man back to prevent a catastrophe his own mission may have caused.
Machine rule two ways: Skynet's open war of extermination against the Matrix's quiet farm.
Both are 1980s visions of civilisation ending soon, one from fuel, one from machines.

worlds.setting: A twentieth-century astronaut splashes down after two thousand years of time dilation and finds an Earth where apes talk, write, ride and rule, and human beings cannot speak. Ape society is a caste order: gorillas command the army, orangutans hold the law and the faith, chimpanzees are tolerated as scientists, and humans are livestock, pets and field labour. Its written history says humans were vermin who destroyed their own world and that apes inherited it - and the sacred scrolls make that account a matter of doctrine.
worlds.conflict: Ape civilisation rests on the teaching that humans were beasts who ruined the planet, so every astronaut who arrives from that world is evidence against scripture. The state's chief scientist knows the truth and suppresses it, the human will not stop talking, and the ape who befriends him goes on trial for heresy. The engine is that contradiction, and the evidence keeps washing up on the beach.
worlds.politics: Ape City is governed by an orangutan establishment that holds the law, the ministry and the sacred scrolls, with gorilla officers commanding the army and chimpanzees confined to the laboratories. Humans have no legal standing at all - mute, hunted, bought and bred - and dissent within the ape order is prosecuted as heresy rather than as politics.
worlds.technology: Deliberately pre-industrial: horses, carts, muskets, oil lamps, paper, windmills and competent surgery, with no engines, electricity or flight anywhere in ape society. The only advanced technology on the planet is what falls out of the sky - a spacecraft, a speaking doll, a buried weapon - and the authorities' first instinct is to confiscate or destroy it. The Forbidden Zone is still radioactive.
worlds.mood: Sun-bleached, hierarchical, unsettling - an adventure story that keeps turning into an argument about who is allowed to know what happened.

whereToStart.title: Rise of the Planet of the Apes

whereToStart.title: Planet of the Apes

Both begin in a recognisable twentieth century and end on a plague-stripped Earth.
Two futures built on the radioactive ruins of the twentieth century and its monuments.

worlds.setting: The oil ran out and the war for what was left finished the job. Australia is a desert of stripped towns, burnt highways and tribes that trade in petrol; there is no government, no money worth having, and almost no machine that still runs. A former policeman drives a modified V8 through it. The films get sparser as they go: the first still has courts, hospitals and a police budget, the second is one refinery, the third a methane town, the fourth a single chase across a salt plain.
worlds.conflict: Fuel is the currency and everyone is either guarding a supply or taking one. Against that, the fiction keeps asking what is worth keeping: a tanker of petrol, a cage of pigs, a handful of seeds, a green place that may already be gone. Max is the constant: a man who wants to be left alone, dragged into other people's attempts to build something that outlasts the week.
worlds.politics: There is no state. Power belongs to whoever controls a resource and has the vehicles to defend it: a refinery tribe, a town that runs on pig methane and settles disputes in a cage, a citadel that rations water from a pipe. Authority is personal, local and temporary, and the strongest institution left in the first film is a police force of four cars.
worlds.technology: Salvage-level mechanical. V8 engines are kept alive by cannibalising everything else, and the rest is crossbows, shotguns, petrol bombs, wire and welding. Nothing is manufactured and nothing is replaced; the fetish objects are a supercharged interceptor, a tanker, a war rig and fuel itself. Medicine, aviation and electronics have effectively stopped, and a working vehicle is a form of wealth.
worlds.mood: Austere, sun-cooked, elegiac - the end of the world told through car chases, with very little dialogue and even less hope.
themes: the road as the only society
the man who will not be owned

Both are 1980s stories of the world ending soon, one from thirst, one from machines.
Both strip civilisation down to scavenging among the ruins of recognisably our own cities.

worlds.setting: On Saturday 23 October 2077 the bombs fell and the world ended in about two hours. The America that died had never moved past the 1950s: it was a country of diners, atomic cars, civil-defence drills and cheerful corporate advertising, and its ruins are still full of all three - robots polishing floors, broadcasters reading old news, billboards for products nobody makes. The survivors came out of Vault-Tec vaults that were never really shelters: each vault was a secret sociological experiment performed on the people sealed inside.
worlds.conflict: The old world will not stay dead and the new one cannot agree on what to build. The Enclave claims to be the legitimate United States, the Brotherhood of Steel wants dangerous technology locked away, the Institute manufactures synthetic people, and the New California Republic is attempting a republic. Everyone with a plan turns out to be running an experiment on somebody, which is the wasteland's one reliable political tradition.
worlds.politics: No government survives the war. What replaces it is a patchwork: the New California Republic with a senate and a bureaucracy, Caesar's Legion as a slaver army modelled on Rome, the Brotherhood of Steel as a militarised technology cult, and the Enclave as the pre-war state's surviving remnant. Vault-Tec's contracts and old corporate AIs still exercise power long after the country that chartered them ceased to exist.
worlds.technology: Retro-futurist and broken: fusion-powered cars, laser and plasma weapons, Power Armor, robots with personalities, and computers that run on tape and green text. Everything is 1950s Americana with atomic power, and everything is falling apart, so the economy runs on bottle caps and the most valuable skill is knowing how to repair the twentieth century.
worlds.mood: Satirical, brutal, absurd - the end of the world with a jukebox playing, where horror and comedy arrive in the same scene.

connections.note: The two poles of post-apocalyptic fiction: austere Australia against Fallout's satirical, over-stuffed wasteland.
Both end the world with a nuclear exchange; one blames the machines, one blames the powers.
Both build a future on the radioactive ruins of the twentieth century and its buried monuments.

worlds.setting: Most human beings live in a city that looks like 1999 and cannot leave it: offices, payphones, noodle bars, the same year running on a loop, with work, rent and weather. Their bodies lie in pods and their heat is fed into the machines' power supply, and almost nobody inside knows. The simulation is not a puzzle or a prison; it is a place to live, built to be believed. Outside, the sky is black with nanites and the last free city is underground.
worlds.conflict: The machines need the pods to keep running and the people inside them docile, so the system is built to be believed; the humans who wake up need it destroyed, so the war is fought over what people will accept as real. Every cycle the machines offer one chosen person the same bargain, and every cycle the resistance must decide whether freeing humanity is worth ending it.
worlds.politics: The Machines are the state: a city of programs that governs a farm of human beings, with the Architect, the Oracle and the central intelligence managing the simulation and its cycles. Among humans, Zion is a militarised city-state run by a council and its ship captains, and the rogue programs inside the Matrix - exiles, Agents, the Merovingian - have a politics of their own that matters more than any human government.
worlds.technology: Inside, the technology is exactly 1999: landlines, pagers, CRT monitors and hard-wired telephones, because the simulation was built from the last human world and never updated. Outside, the real world runs on hovercraft, EMP weapons and pods; the machines build in black chrome, and the most powerful tool anyone has is the ability to rewrite the simulation's rules from within it.
worlds.mood: Cool, paranoid, vertiginous - a martial-arts action film with a philosophy seminar underneath and a permanently black sky overhead.
themes: the chosen one as a mechanism

Dick's nested realities are the Matrix's ancestors: a true world hidden behind a false one.

worlds.setting: Two worlds, thirty-nine years apart, and the same loop between them. In 1996 the present is ordinary - Baltimore, Philadelphia, telephones, airports, a psychiatrist's office - and a man keeps being arrested there for insisting the future has already happened. In 2035 the five billion who died are a precondition of daily life: the survivors live sealed underground in Philadelphia, the surface is a ruined city nobody visits, and the scientists who run the compound send convicts up as scouts because no one else can be spared.
worlds.conflict: A laboratory-grown virus released in Philadelphia in December 1996 kills five billion people within a year, and by 2035 the survivors' only project is reaching back to recover a pure sample of it. The men they send arrive in the wrong years, are locked up as lunatics and cannot warn anyone who would believe them; the message that sends them back was left by the people they went to find.
worlds.politics: In 2035 authority belongs to the scientists and soldiers who run the sealed compounds, and it is absolute because the only alternative is the surface; dissidents and prisoners are volunteered into the time programme and are the state's raw material. In 1996 the institutions are ordinary - police, hospitals, psychiatry - and their ordinary procedures are precisely what defeats the warning.
worlds.technology: 1996 is our 1996 exactly: payphones, answering machines, a handheld voice recorder, a revolver, an airport departure lounge. 2035 is not futuristic so much as stripped: decontamination chambers, sealed dormitories, wall screens, a time-displacement chair assembled from scavenged equipment, and a laboratory culturing the virus it cannot cure. There are no robots and no flying cars; the future's technology is a chair and a needle.
worlds.mood: Bleak, clammy, obsessive - a plague film, an asylum film and a time-travel film at once, played for sadness rather than spectacle.

connections.note: Both send a man back to stop a catastrophe his own mission may be helping to cause.
Both futures treat people as raw material: convicts as scouts, bodies as batteries.
Both begin in a recognisable twentieth century and end in the ruins of it.
